title: Linux Filesystem, Permissions and Users: Quick Revision
summary: Revision notes on the Linux directory layout, paths, everyday file commands, permissions (rwx, octal, chmod, chown), users, groups, sudo and links. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Filesystem Hierarchy and Paths
points: Everything hangs off one tree rooted at / (no drive letters); devices and disks are mounted into it
Key dirs: /etc config, /var logs and changing data, /home user files, /usr installed programs, /tmp scratch, /dev devices, /proc kernel and process info
Absolute path starts with / (/var/log/syslog); relative path starts from the current directory (../logs)
Shortcuts: . is current dir, .. is parent, ~ is your home, - is the previous dir (cd -)
Mistake: paths are case-sensitive and spaces need quotes or backslash (cd "My Docs"); a leading dot hides a file (.bashrc)

chapters.title: Everyday File Commands: ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, find
points: ls -lah: long format, all files including hidden, human-readable sizes; pwd prints where you are
cp -r copies directories (cp -r src/ dest/); cp -a also keeps permissions and timestamps
mv both moves and renames (mv old.txt new.txt); it never needs -r for directories
rm -r deletes recursively with no trash and no undo; rm -rf /path/ is the danger line, so check with ls first
find /var -name "*.log" -mtime -1 -type f finds by name, age and type; add -exec rm {} \; to act on results; unlike locate it walks the live disk

chapters.title: Permissions: rwx and Octal
points: ls -l shows -rwxr-xr-- : type char, then owner, group, others triplets
r=4, w=2, x=1, so rwx=7, r-x=5, rw-=6, r--=4; 640 means owner rw, group r, others none
On files x means executable; on directories x means can cd into it and r means can list names
chmod works in octal (chmod 755 script.sh) or symbolic (chmod u+x file, g-w, o=r, a+r)
Mistake: chmod 777 as a fix opens the file to everyone; give the exact bit needed. Use chmod -R carefully: a mode like chmod -R 755 also sets x on plain files (use X to add x to directories only)

chapters.title: Users, Groups, chown and sudo
points: Each file has one owner user and one owner group; check yours with id and whoami; accounts live in /etc/passwd and /etc/group
chown alice:devs file changes owner and group (root only); chown -R recurses; chgrp changes the group only
Add a user to a group with usermod -aG docker alice; without -a the user is removed from every other group; log in again to apply
sudo runs one command as root using your own password, if you are listed in /etc/sudoers; sudo -i opens a root shell; edit the list only with visudo
Mistake: sudo before everything leaves root-owned files in your home; prefer fixing ownership with chown over running as root. sudo echo x > f fails because the redirect runs as you, so use tee

chapters.title: Links: Hard vs Symbolic
points: Every file name points to an inode (the file's metadata and pointers to its data blocks); a link is another name or pointer to it
Hard link: ln target link adds a second name for the same inode; the data survives until the last name is deleted
Symbolic link: ln -s target link is a small file holding a path; it breaks (dangling) if the target is moved or deleted
Hard links cannot cross filesystems or point to directories; symlinks can do both and are shown as l in ls -l with an arrow ->
Mistake: ln -s argument order is target first, then link name; a relative symlink target is resolved from the link's folder, not your current directory

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Files, Permissions, Users and Links
points: Navigate and list: pwd, cd -, ls -lah, tree -L 2; paths: / absolute, ../ parent, ~ home
Manage: cp -a src dst, mv old new, rm -r dir, mkdir -p a/b/c, touch f; find . -name "*.py" -type f
Octal table: 7 rwx, 6 rw-, 5 r-x, 4 r--, 0 ---; common modes: 644 files, 755 scripts and dirs, 600 secrets (SSH keys), 700 private dirs
Ownership and access: chmod u+x f, chown user:group f, usermod -aG group user, id, sudo -i, visudo
Links: ln target hard, ln -s target link symbolic; ls -li shows inode numbers; readlink -f resolves a symlink
